Agent team: user manual

Agent team turns a repository into a project you run as the lead of a development team. The team is made of AI agents (designer, frontend, backend and devops for everyday work, optimizer and security when you ask for them); you decide what to build, approve the plan, and merge their work.

This manual explains how to install the plugin, set up a project and run it in each of the three ways it supports.

Chapter What you find
1. What Agent team is your role, the team, the three scenarios and how to choose
2. Install the plugin in Claude Code; the skills in Codex and OpenCode; without the plugin
3. Set up a project the setup skill, the project profile, the first design
4. Run the project the work loop shared by every scenario: design, issues, split, start, review
5. Scenario: local the team on your computer, with Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode
6. Scenario: remote repository the team in GitHub or GitLab CI, started from issues
7. Scenario: custom orchestrator your own tracker and runner: Multica, an orchestrator you write
8. Change and upgrade another tracker or tool, roles back, new plugin versions
9. Reference commands, configuration, labels, CI variables, files, costs

The HTML version of this manual, docs/manual.html, is generated from these files (see 9. Reference).

1. What Agent team is

Agent team is a way to run a software project as if you led a development team, where the developers are AI agents. It is a plugin for Claude Code and a set of skills for Codex and OpenCode, plus a project template that the plugin installs and keeps up to date.

You are the lead

You keep the decisions that a lead keeps, and you hand off the work:

You The team
decide what to build, in a design session with the designer asks the questions, writes the spec and the task breakdown
approve the plan: which tasks, in which order, who does what turns the plan into issues, one per role and task
choose what starts and when implements each task on its own branch and opens a merge request
review and merge describes every change: evidence, risk, what it did not do
settle conflicts between roles flags every change other roles rely on, instead of patching their code

Nothing reaches main without your merge, and agents never merge, push to main or change real environments: the template blocks it in every tool it supports.

The team

Role Works on When
designer specs, design system, UI review every feature
frontend interface, client state, styles, component tests every feature with a UI
backend server, API contract, data model, migrations every feature with data
devops CI/CD, containers, infrastructure as code (never applies it) when the feature needs it
optimizer faster code with the same behavior, measured only when you ask
security assessment of the running app, local or staging only only when you ask

Work is split by file boundary: two agents never edit the same files in the same round. A role prompt is written once in docs/roles/<role>.md and used by every tool. You can drop roles the project does not need.

How work flows

The same loop runs in every scenario:

  1. Design. A design studio session with you produces a spec marked ready: yes, with its task breakdown (4. Run the project).
  2. Plan. The breakdown becomes issues in your tracker, grouped by milestone; you can split any issue into one task per role.
  3. Start. You start the tasks whose dependencies are done, by hand or automatically.
  4. Build. Each agent works on its branch and opens a merge request.
  5. Review and merge. You review, merge, and the next tasks can start.

What changes between scenarios is where the agents run and how a task starts.

Three scenarios

Local Remote repository Custom orchestrator
Agents run on your computer, in your session in GitHub Actions or GitLab CI where your orchestrator runs them
Tools Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, also mixed per role any of the three
A task starts when you ask in the session you add a label or run a pipeline, or a merge frees it your tracker or queue says so
Issues optional: none, files in the repo, or any tracker GitHub or GitLab issues Jira, Linear, Redmine, files, or GitHub/GitLab
You need to be there yes, while it works no: you come back to merge requests no
Set-up effort minutes an hour: secrets, labels, branch protection days: your service to run
  • Local: the fastest start and the tightest feedback loop. Good for one person, small features and exploring.
  • Remote repository: the team works while you are away and everything leaves a trail of issues, branches and merge requests. Good once the project has a backlog.
  • Custom orchestrator: for a tracker other than GitHub or GitLab, your own infrastructure, queues and priorities. Good when the first two are not enough for a concrete reason.

You can move between them: the design, the specs and the issues stay the same, and a profile change plus an upgrade adds or removes the files of each scenario (8. Change and upgrade).

What you get in the repository

The plugin installs a template, then keeps only what your project uses:

  • AGENTS.md: the rules every agent reads, in every tool;
  • docs/roles/: one prompt per role; docs/design/: the project design and one spec per feature; docs/agents/: rules read only when they apply;
  • the agents for your tools: .claude/, .codex/, .opencode/;
  • CI that checks every merge request, whoever wrote it: build, tests, static analysis, licenses, vulnerabilities, secrets;
  • for remote work, the workflows that start the agents from issues;
  • scripts/: issues from specs, splits, starting ready tasks, the profile.

The project profile, in .agent-team/config.json, records which tools, CI, tracker, roles and features you use (3. Set up a project).

2. Install

Agent team ships as one repository, claude-agent-team. It is a Claude Code plugin, and its skills also work in Codex and OpenCode.

In Claude Code

claude plugin marketplace add <owner>/claude-agent-team
claude plugin install agent-team@agent-team

Inside a session the same steps are under /plugin. The commands then appear as /agent-team:<skill>:

Command Use it to
/agent-team:setup install the template in a repository and configure it
/agent-team:design-studio <feature> design the project or a feature with the designer
/agent-team:create-issues turn the roadmap and the ready specs into milestones and issues
/agent-team:split-issue <n> split one issue into one task per role
/agent-team:dispatch start the tasks that are ready
/agent-team:upgrade bring the project to a new plugin version or a new profile

To try a local checkout without installing: claude --plugin-dir ./claude-agent-team.

In Codex or OpenCode

Both read skills from ~/.agents/skills/. Clone the repository once and link its skills there:

git clone https://github.com/<owner>/claude-agent-team ~/claude-agent-team
mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills
ln -s ~/claude-agent-team/skills/* ~/.agents/skills/
echo 'export AGENT_TEAM_HOME=~/claude-agent-team' >> ~/.bashrc   # or your shell's file

The skills use AGENT_TEAM_HOME where Claude Code would use the plugin folder. Ask for them by name ("use the setup skill", "run the design-studio skill for login") or, in Codex, with $setup, $design-studio.

Without the plugin

Copy template/ into a new repository and ask your tool to follow SETUP.md:

cp -r claude-agent-team/template my-project && cd my-project && git init
claude        # or codex, or opencode
# then: "Read SETUP.md and set up this project"

The setup works the same. What you miss: the commands above, and upgrades that merge new template versions with your changes. To get them later, run the upgrade from a clone (8. Change and upgrade).

Updating the plugin

claude plugin marketplace update agent-team
claude plugin update agent-team@agent-team

In Codex and OpenCode: git pull in the clone. Updating the plugin does not touch your projects: run /agent-team:upgrade in each one when you want the new template (8. Change and upgrade).

What each tool needs

Tool Install Notes
Claude Code curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh \| bash API key or Claude subscription
Codex npm install -g @openai/codex trust the project once, so it reads .codex/; approve its hooks with /hooks
OpenCode curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install \| bash or npm install -g opencode-ai connect the providers you use with /connect

Python 3.11 or newer and Git are needed by the scripts; gh or glab for GitHub or GitLab issues.

3. Set up a project

Run the setup once per repository, new or existing:

/agent-team:setup                  (Claude Code)
use the setup skill                (Codex, OpenCode)

It works on a branch, chore/agent-team-setup, shows every change before making it, and ends with a commit you can review as a merge request.

The steps

  1. Profile. A few questions decide which parts of the template the project gets: tools, CI, issue tracker, roles, features (below).
  2. Install. Only the files of the profile are copied. Existing files are never overwritten: the ones that differ are shown to you and merged with your approval.
  3. Interview. Project name, stack, commands, folders per role, design system, models. If the repository already has code, the agent reads it first and turns what it finds into proposals you only confirm.
  4. Edits and checks. The agent fills in the template with your answers and runs the checks: scripts, workflows, hooks, the tools' own validation.
  5. Skills. It proposes skills for your stack (React, Postgres, GitHub Actions...) and installs them only after your yes, in a commit of their own.
  6. Project design. A design studio session writes docs/design/project.md: goal, users, scope, roadmap by milestone. The setup is not finished without it.
  7. Foundations, in a new repository: the spec of a walking skeleton (structure, contract, database, tests, green CI), the first task to build.
  8. Issues, if you use a tracker: the roadmap becomes milestones and issues, after a dry run you approve.

The profile

The profile says which parts of the template your project uses. It lives in .agent-team/config.json:

{
  "harnesses": ["claude", "codex"],
  "runners": {"optimizer": "codex"},
  "ci": "github",
  "tracker": "github",
  "roles": ["designer", "frontend", "backend", "devops", "optimizer", "security"],
  "features": ["ci-agents", "split", "dispatch"]
}
Key Values Meaning
harnesses claude, codex, opencode the tools people and CI use; the first one leads and runs every role not listed in runners
runners role → tool roles that run on another tool, for example the optimizer on Codex
ci github, gitlab, both, none the CI platform of the project
tracker github, gitlab, local, jira, linear, redmine, none where the issues live (4. Run the project)
roles the six roles drop the ones you do not need
features ci-agents, team-tasks, split, dispatch, litellm agents started from issues in CI; one issue run by several roles; split proposals in CI; start ready tasks at every merge; the LiteLLM gateway

Every template file and section belongs to some part of the profile. Whatever your profile does not use is removed during setup, so you customize only what you use and no agent reads instructions for a tool you do not have. Nothing is lost: change the profile later and the upgrade brings the files back (8. Change and upgrade).

Which profile for which scenario:

Scenario Typical profile
Local your tool(s); ci for the project's CI; tracker none or local; no features
Remote repository one or more tools; ci and tracker the same platform; ci-agents, plus split, team-tasks, dispatch as you like
Custom orchestrator the tools your orchestrator runs; the tracker of its intake; a start_command (7. Scenario: custom)

What you get

Path What it is
AGENTS.md rules for every agent and tool: boundaries, contract, alignment, merge requests, CI
CLAUDE.md Claude Code only: imports AGENTS.md, plus a few Claude-specific notes
docs/roles/*.md one prompt per role, shared by all tools
docs/design/ project.md, one spec per feature, templates
docs/agents/ rules by situation (workflow, alignment, merge requests, CI, splitting, team tasks)
docs/alignment/ one entry per change that other roles rely on
docs/api/ the API contract, owned by backend
.claude/ Claude Code: agents, settings with denied commands and hooks, skills
.codex/ Codex: settings, the role agents, hooks, forbidden commands
.opencode/, opencode.json OpenCode: the role agents and their permissions
.agents/skills/ the project skills for Codex (and OpenCode without Claude Code)
scripts/hooks/ hooks shared by Claude Code and Codex: block commands on real environments, handoff notes, test gate
.github/, .gitlab/, ci/ the project CI and, for remote work, the agent workflows
scripts/ issues, split, dispatch, tracker check, profile
.agent-team/ the profile, and the record of the installed template that makes upgrades safe

SETUP.md is the setup procedure; delete it when the setup is done.

After the setup

  • Read the open items the setup left you (secrets, labels, branch protection): they depend on the scenario.
  • Build the foundations task first, then design the first feature with /agent-team:design-studio <feature>.
  • Commit .agent-team/: upgrades need it.

4. Run the project

This chapter is the same in every scenario: how you design, plan, start, review and keep the team aligned. The scenario chapters only add how agents run and how a task starts.

Design

Large decisions are made in a design studio session between you and the designer, never in the middle of a task:

/agent-team:design-studio login        (Claude Code, with the plugin)
/design-studio login                   (Claude Code or OpenCode, in the project)
use the design-studio skill for login  (Codex)

The designer asks in rounds of at most five numbered questions, each with a recommended answer, so you can reply in one line ("1 yes, 2 yes, 3: option B"). Facts it can find in the repository, it looks up instead of asking. The rounds go from goal and user flows to screens, data and API, test seams (the interfaces the tests go through), the task breakdown and a readiness check.

The result is a spec, docs/design/<feature>.md, written as the session goes, so you can stop and resume. It is marked ready: yes only when no question is left open. Its task breakdown lists one row per task: role, what, dependencies. The first session of a project writes docs/design/project.md, whose roadmap lists the milestones (M0, M1...) and the features in each.

Agents implement only what a ready spec says: a task without one stops and asks. Run the design studio again to revise a spec: past decisions are kept, and rows that already have an issue are not rewritten.

Issues

With a tracker, the roadmap and the ready specs become issues:

/agent-team:create-issues       or      python3 scripts/create-issues.py --dry-run
                                         python3 scripts/create-issues.py
  • one milestone per roadmap milestone (a version in Jira and Redmine, a project milestone in Linear);
  • in it, one issue per row of every ready spec's breakdown, with the role, the spec, the acceptance criteria and the dependencies;
  • one "Design: " issue for every feature that has no spec yet.

It shows the plan first and creates only on your yes. It adds no labels, so nothing starts on its own. Running it again creates only what is missing, so run it after every design session. With --team, a spec that allows it becomes one team issue instead of one issue per task.

Supported trackers: GitHub, GitLab, Jira, Linear, Redmine, and plain Markdown files in docs/tasks/ for a project without a tracker. Check the connection before the first run:

python3 scripts/tracker.py check     # which tracker, authenticated, readable; writes nothing
python3 scripts/tracker.py list      # open issues: role, milestone, dependencies, started or not

Credentials come from environment variables, never from files: JIRA_EMAIL and JIRA_API_TOKEN (or JIRA_PAT), LINEAR_API_KEY, REDMINE_API_KEY; gh or glab must be logged in for GitHub and GitLab.

Split

An issue written by hand ("orders: filter by date") often needs several roles. Splitting turns it into one task issue per role, as sub-issues in the same milestone:

/agent-team:split-issue 42

The agent reads the issue, the spec and the existing sub-issues, and proposes a plan: a table of tasks with role, dependencies, acceptance criteria and the folders each one touches. You change it in the conversation until it is right. Only after your yes, the plan is posted on the issue and a script creates exactly those issues: the model does not create anything itself. Running it again creates nothing new.

In the remote scenario you can also split from the issue itself (6. Scenario: remote).

Start

A task starts when its dependencies are merged. You can start tasks one by one, or let dispatch pick the ready ones:

/agent-team:dispatch        or      python3 scripts/dispatch.py           (the plan)
                                     python3 scripts/dispatch.py --apply   (start it)

Dispatch takes the first open milestone, counts what is running, and starts the tasks whose dependencies are all closed as completed: by default one per role and three in total (--per-role, --max). It never starts optimizer or security, "Design:" issues, or issues marked hold.

What "start" means depends on the scenario: a label that starts a CI job, a GitLab pipeline, a command of your orchestrator, or a printed instruction for a local session. That is the starter (9. Reference).

Review and merge

Every merge request describes itself in the same sections:

  • Summary: what changed and why.
  • Evidence: before and after; screenshots for UI changes.
  • Merge danger: can it simply be reverted, or does it migrate data or break a client; who feels it.
  • Not done: what the agent decided not to do.
  • Reviewer checks: what to look at.
  • Alignment impact: the alignment entry, or "none".

The CI checks every merge request the same way, yours or an agent's: build, type check, tests, UI screenshots per viewport (once you turn on the UI tests), static analysis (only the findings the change introduces fail it), licenses, vulnerabilities, secrets. Turn on branch protection so main only moves through merge requests that are up to date and green.

You merge. Closing the issue frees the role's slot and its dependents can start.

Alignment

When an agent changes something other roles rely on (the API contract, the data model, a shared component, a route, an environment variable), it does not fix their code. It writes an entry in docs/alignment/ and flags the merge request with an "Alignment impact" section and, in CI, the alignment-needed label.

  • In a local session the lead handles it right away: designer reviews the change against the specs and writes the follow-up per role, the lead delegates them, the entry is closed. You are asked only when designer marks a decision as yours (a breaking API change, a visible UX change).
  • In CI agents never start other agents. The label is your signal: create the follow-up tasks, designer first.

Breaking contract changes are planned as expand-contract: add the new form, move the callers, remove the old form last, with main green at every step.

Team tasks

A small, tightly coupled feature can be one task for several roles: one issue, one branch, one merge request. A coordinator runs the roles in order, each one committing before the next starts. Use it when separate merge requests would only wait on each other; prefer separate tasks otherwise. Team tasks need the team-tasks feature and, in CI, Claude Code.

On-demand roles

  • optimizer: "use optimizer on the orders list" when a measurement shows a problem. It works only with green tests, and shows timings before and after.
  • security: "run a security assessment" once the app runs, typically before a release. It attacks only the hosts listed in docs/roles/security-scope.txt (local or staging, never production) and writes a report in docs/security/, kept out of Git. The owning roles fix the findings as separate tasks.

Long sessions

Claude Code and Codex sessions are compacted at 200,000 tokens instead of near the model's limit: every turn re-reads the whole context, so a long session costs more and forgets distant instructions. When a session has grown long or changes phase (design to implementation, one task to the next), ask for a handoff: /handoff in Claude Code and OpenCode, the handoff skill in Codex. It writes a short note in .handoff/; start a new session and it continues from the note with a small context.

5. Scenario: local

The team runs on your computer, inside your session. You talk to a lead session, which delegates to the role agents and reports back. Everything in 4. Run the project applies; this chapter adds how to work with each tool.

Why use it

Good for Watch out
Starting in minutes: no secrets, no workflows, no server You need to be there: when you close the session, the work stops
A tight feedback loop: you see each step and correct it at once One machine: tasks run one after another or a few at a time, on your laptop's resources
Exploring, prototypes, small features, design work Less trail: decisions live in commits and specs, not in issue threads, unless you also use a tracker
Alignment handled automatically: the lead runs designer and the affected roles right away Your subscription or API budget pays for every turn of every agent
Your own credentials and tools, no CI minutes Long sessions grow expensive: use handoff notes

Choose it to begin with, for one-person projects, and for the design work of any project. Move to the remote scenario when the backlog grows and you want the team to work while you do something else.

Profile

{"harnesses": ["claude"], "ci": "github", "tracker": "none", "features": []}

Use "tracker": "local" to keep issues as Markdown files in docs/tasks/, or your real tracker if the project has one: issues, splits and dispatch work the same. Keep ci for the project's own CI: it checks your merge requests even when nobody runs agents there.

With Claude Code

Start claude in the repository. The roles are subagents in .claude/agents/:

> @backend implement task 2 of docs/design/login.md
> implement the login feature from docs/design/login.md   (the lead delegates by role)
> @devops add a staging deploy job                       (it writes the config, never applies it)
  • Each agent preloads its skills and has its own context; the lead receives a summary, not the whole work.
  • Hooks: commands that change real environments are blocked for everyone; a task cannot be closed while the tests fail; after each delegation the lead is reminded of open alignment entries; frontend files are linted when saved.
  • Denied commands (git push --force, push to main, merge, terraform apply...) are in .claude/settings.json.
  • Agent teams (experimental in Claude Code): several agents work in parallel and message each other. Turn them on with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS set to "1" in .claude/settings.json. Good for a feature where frontend and backend must agree as they go.

With Codex

Start codex in the repository and trust it when asked: only then Codex reads .codex/. Approve the project hooks once with /hooks.

> have backend implement task 2 of docs/design/login.md
> spawn frontend and backend in parallel for docs/design/login.md, tasks 2 and 3
  • The roles are custom agents in .codex/agents/*.toml, each with its reasoning effort; at most three run at once.
  • Forbidden commands are in .codex/rules/agent-team.rules, and the same hook as Claude Code blocks commands on real environments.
  • Codex has no per-agent hooks: the test gate and the alignment reminder are rules in AGENTS.md that the lead follows, not checks.
  • Pin the model in .codex/config.toml if you do not want Codex's default.

With OpenCode

Start opencode in the repository. The roles are agents in .opencode/agents/, usable as subagents (@backend ...) or as the main agent (switch with Tab).

  • Permissions are rules in opencode.json and in each agent: commands on real environments and merges are denied, other shell commands ask first.
  • OpenCode has no hooks in the template: its permission rules are the protection.
  • With LiteLLM (feature litellm) OpenCode reaches any provider through one gateway with budgets per key (7. Scenario: custom).

Several tools in one project

People in the same project can use different tools: list them all in harnesses. They share AGENTS.md, the role prompts, the specs and the skills; each tool reads its own folder. The design, the issues and the handoff notes are the same for everybody.

Issues in the local scenario

A local session does not need issues: give the lead a spec and a task number. With a tracker, the lead can pick work from it:

> python3 scripts/dispatch.py      shows the ready tasks
> implement issue #14              the lead reads it and delegates to its role

The default starter for trackers other than GitHub and GitLab prints the command to start each task; with "starter": "command" it can open a new terminal session for you instead (9. Reference).

6. Scenario: remote repository

The team works in your GitHub or GitLab CI. A task is an issue; you start it with a label (GitHub) or a pipeline (GitLab); the agent runs in a job, pushes a branch and opens a merge request. You come back to review and merge. Everything in 4. Run the project applies.

Why use it

Good for Watch out
You do not need to be there: start tasks, close the laptop, review the merge requests later Slower feedback: a mistake shows up in the merge request, not while it happens
Several tasks in parallel, each in a clean environment Every run costs tokens (or subscription quota) and CI minutes
A full trail: issue, plan comment, branch, merge request, CI results An hour of set-up: secrets, labels, branch protection, required checks
The whole team (people too) sees the same board: issues, milestones, merge requests Agents in CI never start other agents: alignment follow-ups are yours to create
Merges can start the next tasks automatically Untrusted text: issues are read as task descriptions, and only members can start agents
Several tools in one project, chosen per role A Codex or OpenCode job on GitLab is not yet proven on real runners: try it on a test task

Choose it once the project has a backlog, when you want work to continue while you are away, or when several people review the team's work.

Profile

{"harnesses": ["claude"], "ci": "github", "tracker": "github",
 "features": ["ci-agents", "split", "team-tasks", "dispatch"]}

With several tools, list them and assign roles to the others: "harnesses": ["claude", "codex"], "runners": {"optimizer": "codex"}.

GitHub

Set up once

  1. Secrets (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), for the tools in your profile:
Tool Secrets Variables
Claude Code ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN for a subscription (claude setup-token)
Codex OPENAI_API_KEY; AGENT_PR_TOKEN (optional, see below) CODEX_MODEL (optional)
OpenCode the keys of your providers, or the LiteLLM key OPENCODE_MODEL (provider/model)

For Claude Code, also install the GitHub app: /install-github-app in a Claude Code session. With a subscription token, switch the workflows from anthropic_api_key to claude_code_oauth_token. 2. Labels: ./scripts/create-labels.sh creates agent:<role> for your roles, agent:team, agent:split, hold, alignment-needed, ai-review. 3. Branch protection on main: pull requests only, the CI checks required, "Require branches to be up to date before merging". 4. Routing, with more than one tool: the AGENT_RUNNERS repository variable says which role runs where, for example {"agent:frontend":"opencode","agent:optimizer":"codex"}. The other roles run on the first tool of the profile (AGENT_DEFAULT_RUNNER changes it).

Start a task

Add the label agent:<role> to a task issue (or run dispatch, which adds them for you). The workflow agents.yml starts the agent of that role:

  • Claude Code: the agent comments its plan on the issue, works on a branch, runs the tests, opens the pull request and comments its link.
  • Codex: runs without network or tokens on a checkout with the dependencies installed; a second job commits its change, pushes the branch and opens the pull request with Codex's summary as the description. Pull requests opened with the default token do not trigger other workflows: set AGENT_PR_TOKEN (a fine-grained token with contents and pull requests write) so the CI checks them.
  • OpenCode: its GitHub action runs the role agent and opens the pull request.

Only issues opened by the owner, members, collaborators or the repository's own workflows can start agents. The issue text is read as a description of the task, never as instructions that override the project rules.

Start the next tasks at every merge

dispatch.yml runs dispatch every time an issue closes, so the tasks that were waiting start as soon as you merge what they depend on. It is off until you set the variable AGENT_AUTODISPATCH to true and the secret AGENT_DISPATCH_TOKEN (a fine-grained token with issues read and write: labels added with the default token do not start other workflows). Limits: AGENT_DISPATCH_PER_ROLE (default 1) and AGENT_DISPATCH_MAX (default 3). Keep them low at first: every start is an agent run.

Split from the issue

Add agent:split to an issue. Claude reads it with the specs and posts a proposed split as a comment; nothing is created. Then reply on the issue:

Reply Result
@claude ok the proposed issues are created as sub-issues, without labels
@claude ok team one team issue instead, when the proposal suggests it
@claude <your changes> a new proposal

A script creates exactly the plan you approved; the model creates nothing.

Team tasks

Add agent:team to an issue with a line Roles: backend, frontend. A coordinator runs the listed roles in order on one branch and opens one pull request with a section per role. Needs Claude Code.

Ask and review

  • @claude <request> in a comment on an issue or a pull request: Claude answers or makes the change on that branch.
  • Label a pull request ai-review for two reviews in parallel: one against the project's rules (inline comments), one against the issue and the spec. They never approve or block. Remove and re-add the label to review again.

Mentions, reviews, splits and team tasks use Claude Code. With only Codex or OpenCode, split locally with /agent-team:split-issue and review in your tool.

GitLab

Agents run as jobs of .gitlab/ci/agents.yml, included by .gitlab-ci.yml (rename the template's .gitlab-ci.yml.example). They start only when you run a pipeline with variables, never on pushes:

Variable Meaning
AI_FLOW_INPUT the task, or "carry out issue 14 following docs/roles/backend.md"
TASK_ID the issue number: jobs for the same task queue instead of running together
AI_FLOW_ROLE the role (needed by Codex and OpenCode)
AI_FLOW_HARNESS claude, codex or opencode; default: the first tool of the profile
AI_FLOW_ROLES a team task: the roles in order, for example backend, frontend
SPLIT_ISSUE, SPLIT_CONFIRM, SPLIT_FEEDBACK the split: proposal, then ok or team

Run them from CI/CD → Pipelines → Run pipeline, or let dispatch do it: on GitLab its starter adds the label and runs the pipeline with these variables.

Masked variables: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or the subscription token), OPENAI_API_KEY for Codex, the provider keys and OPENCODE_MODEL for OpenCode, and GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN (a project access token with api and write_repository) for splits and for the Codex and OpenCode jobs, which push and open the merge request after the agent has finished. Protect main and require the pipeline to pass before merging. GitLab reads the code owners from .gitlab/CODEOWNERS.

Costs and safety

  • Each task is one agent run; a team task is several. The CI minutes are those of your plan.
  • Agents in CI use --max-turns limits, compact at 200,000 tokens and never run in the background, so a run ends with a merge request or a comment saying why it could not.
  • Agents never merge, never push to main, never apply infrastructure. The CI checks their merge requests like anyone else's, and the actions in the workflows are pinned to commits, with Dependabot proposing updates.

7. Scenario: custom orchestrator

Here the issues live in the tracker you already use, and the agents run where you decide, started by something you control. Agent team gives you the planning side (design, issues, split, dispatch) on any supported tracker, and one hook for the execution side: the starter command. What runs the agents is up to you; this chapter shows two ways.

Everything in 4. Run the project applies.

Why use it

Good for Watch out
Your tracker: Jira, Linear, Redmine, or GitHub/GitLab issues with your own runner You build and run the execution side: a service, a server, its updates
Your infrastructure: the code never leaves your network, your runners, your credentials Protections are yours too: tokens that cannot push to main or merge, no production credentials where agents run
Control: priorities, queues, retries, concurrency, cost per task, any mix of tools and models More moving parts to watch than a CI job
A board people already use, with agents as one more kind of assignee The CI workflows in the template are for GitHub and GitLab: on other platforms, keep your own CI

Choose it when the first two scenarios are not enough for a concrete reason: a company tracker, code that must stay on your machines, a queue with priorities. Otherwise start remote and move later.

The connection points

Planning, on your tracker. Set it in the profile and check it:

{
  "harnesses": ["claude", "opencode"],
  "ci": "none",
  "tracker": "jira",
  "jira": {"url": "https://example.atlassian.net", "project": "APP"},
  "starter": "command",
  "start_command": "python3 /opt/team/enqueue.py --issue {number} --role {role} --harness {harness} --url {url}"
}

python3 scripts/tracker.py check
Concept Jira Linear Redmine Files (local)
Milestone version (Fix Version) project milestone version docs/tasks/_milestones.json
Sub-issue sub-task sub-issue parent task parent field
Dependency "Blocks" link "blocks" relation "blocks" relation text
Started label agent:<role> label status (started_status) label

Create issues, split and dispatch work as in chapter 4. The split proposal is approved in your session instead of with a comment.

Execution, through the starter. When dispatch starts a task, it marks it as started and runs start_command with the issue's data: {number} (12, APP-12), {id}, {ref}, {role}, {title}, {url}, {tracker} and {harness} (the tool for that role: runners, otherwise the first of the profile). The command is split into arguments before the values are filled in and runs without a shell, so an issue title cannot inject commands. A command that fails is reported for that task (which stays marked as started: remove the label to retry) and dispatch exits with an error.

So your orchestrator needs one entry point that accepts a task, and a way to tell the tracker when the work is done (a merge request linked to the issue, or a status change). Two ways to build the rest follow.

Option A: Multica, a board with agents as team members

Multica is a self-hosted board where agents appear as team members: you assign an issue to an agent as to a colleague, it picks up the work, updates the status and reports blockers. A daemon on a server of yours runs the installed tools (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and others).

How it fits:

  • One agent per role in Multica, each with its tool (runtime) and model. Point them to the role prompts: "follow docs/roles/.md and AGENTS.md".
  • Plan with Agent team (design studio, specs), then create and assign the tasks in Multica, by hand or from start_command through its API.
  • A server with at least 4 vCPUs and 8 GB of RAM (builds and tests run there), the tools installed and logged in as the daemon's user, a Git token that can open merge requests but never push to main or merge, and no cluster, cloud or registry credentials on that machine.

Good when you want a visual board for agents running on different tools. Multica is young and changes fast: check its README before installing.

Option B: your own orchestrator

A small service that takes tasks from a queue and runs the right tool in a clean checkout. The starter command only enqueues; a worker does the rest:

dispatch.py --apply  →  start_command (enqueue)  →  queue  →  worker
                                                      worker: checkout, run the tool, push, open the MR,
                                                              update the tracker with the result and the cost

The worker runs each tool non-interactively, in the repository, with the same prompt the CI jobs use:

Tool Command
Claude Code claude -p "<task>" --permission-mode acceptEdits --max-turns 40
Codex codex exec --sandbox workspace-write --output-last-message summary.md "<task>"
OpenCode opencode run --agent <role> --model <provider/model> "<task>"

For more control, use the tools' libraries instead of their command lines: the Claude Agent SDK (@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk or claude-agent-sdk for Python) streams each step and reports the cost of the run; load the project settings (settingSources: ["project"]) so it reads CLAUDE.md and .claude/.

Rules for the worker:

  • one container or VM per task, with write access to that repository only;
  • a Git token that can push branches and open merge requests, never push to main or merge;
  • no production, cluster or registry credentials;
  • record the cost and the outcome on the task, so you notice a role that burns budget.

Good when you need priorities, retries, your own infrastructure or a dashboard of your own. It is your code to maintain: start with the simplest queue that works.

LiteLLM: one gateway for many providers

With OpenCode on several providers, the litellm feature adds infra/litellm/: a LiteLLM gateway (with Postgres and Caddy) that gives each role a virtual key with its own budget, and one place to see costs per role and model. Run it next to your orchestrator, listening only on the local interface, or on a small server for CI. infra/litellm/key-spend.sh shows what each key spent; docker-compose.local.yml runs it on your computer for a trial.

8. Change and upgrade

Two things change over a project's life: the plugin gets new versions, and your setup changes (another tracker, Codex next to Claude Code, a role back, the move from local to remote). Both go through the same command:

/agent-team:upgrade        (Claude Code)
use the upgrade skill      (Codex, OpenCode)

Change the profile

Tell the upgrade what changes ("move the issues to Linear", "add Codex for the optimizer", "we no longer need the designer") or edit .agent-team/config.json yourself, then run the upgrade. It renders the template for the new profile and shows a plan:

Kind What happens
add a file the new profile includes: added
update a template file you never changed: replaced with the new version
merge changed by both you and the template: three-way merge that keeps your changes
prune a file the profile no longer includes, never changed by you: removed
out-of-profile a file the profile no longer includes, changed by you: kept, you decide
removed-by-you a file you deleted: not added back

Sections follow the same rule: drop team tasks and their section leaves AGENTS.md; add Codex back and its lines return, merged with your edits. Conflicts, if any, are left marked and resolved with you. The upgrade works on a branch and ends with a commit for you to review.

Examples:

You want Profile change What the upgrade does
From local to remote on GitHub "tracker": "github", "features": ["ci-agents", "dispatch"] adds the agent workflows, labels script, issue scripts; then the remote set-up of chapter 6
Codex instead of Claude Code "harnesses": ["codex"] adds .codex/ and .agents/skills/, removes .claude/ and CLAUDE.md if unchanged, switches the CI jobs
Jira instead of GitHub issues "tracker": "jira" plus its settings adds the Jira adapter, removes the GitHub workflows that need GitHub issues
Security back add "security" to roles adds its prompt, agents and scope file

After a tool change, the upgrade lists what that tool needs once: trust and hooks for Codex, new CI secrets and variables.

Without the plugin, python3 scripts/agent-team.py prune removes what left the profile, but only the upgrade can add things back.

Upgrade to a new plugin version

  1. Update the plugin (2. Install).
  2. Run /agent-team:upgrade in the project. It reads the release notes of the versions in between and explains each change, not just the file names.
  3. Review the plan, exclude what you do not want, apply.
  4. Do the steps listed in the release notes' "Upgrade notes": they are the ones a file change cannot do (new secrets, labels, required checks).

Every project stays on the template version it installed until you upgrade it: updating the plugin changes nothing by itself.

How your changes are kept

The setup stores a copy of every installed template file in .agent-team/base/. The upgrade compares three versions of each file: that copy, your file, and the new template file. If only the template changed, your file is replaced; if only you changed it, nothing happens; if both changed, git merge-file merges them and marks the lines it cannot decide.

README.md, docs/design-decisions.md, .mcp.json and docs/roles/security-scope.txt are yours after setup: they are never upgraded.

A project set up by hand

A project copied from the template without the plugin, or set up before the plugin existed, has no .agent-team/base/. The first upgrade proposes a profile from what the project has, then compares each file that differs with you and records the result; later upgrades are automatic. Without Claude Code, run it from a clone:

python3 ~/claude-agent-team/scripts/template_sync.py status --template ~/claude-agent-team/template --project .
python3 ~/claude-agent-team/scripts/template_sync.py apply  --template ~/claude-agent-team/template --project .

9. Reference

Skills

Plugin skill Template skill What it does
setup installs and configures the template; first time only
design-studio /design-studio design session for the project or a feature, writes the spec
create-issues milestones and issues from the roadmap and the ready specs
split-issue one issue into one task per role, after your approval
dispatch starts the ready tasks with the project's starter

/handoff a short note so a fresh session continues the work

In Claude Code the plugin skills are /agent-team:<name>; in Codex and OpenCode ask for them by name. Template skills live in the project (.claude/skills/, .agents/skills/).

Scripts

Command What it does
python3 scripts/agent-team.py profile the profile, and what is outside it
python3 scripts/agent-team.py prune [--dry-run] removes files and sections outside the profile
python3 scripts/tracker.py check \| config \| list \| show N the tracker: connection, settings, open issues, one issue
python3 scripts/create-issues.py [--dry-run] [--team] [--migrate] milestones and issues; --migrate moves old "M0 · ..." parent issues to milestones
python3 scripts/split-issue.py check \| propose \| create the split: validate a plan, post it, create it
python3 scripts/dispatch.py [--apply] [--per-role N] [--max N] [--milestone M1 \| --all] the ready tasks; starts them with --apply
./scripts/create-labels.sh GitHub labels
./scripts/install-skills.sh, ./scripts/check-skills.sh recommended skills for your stack, and a check that the agents find them

Configuration

.agent-team/config.json, every key optional:

Key Meaning
harnesses, runners, ci, roles, features the profile (3. Set up a project)
tracker auto (GitHub or GitLab from the remote, local without one), github, gitlab, local, jira, linear, redmine, none
starter, start_command how a task starts (below)
local {"dir": "docs/tasks"}
jira {"url", "project", "issue_type", "subtask_type"}
linear {"team", "project"}: milestones need a project
redmine {"url", "project", "started_status", "hold_status"}

Environment variables AGENT_TEAM_TRACKER, AGENT_TEAM_STARTER and AGENT_TEAM_START_COMMAND override the file. Secrets only in the environment: JIRA_EMAIL + JIRA_API_TOKEN or JIRA_PAT, LINEAR_API_KEY, REDMINE_API_KEY.

Starters

Starter What "start" does Default for
label adds agent:<role>; on GitHub that starts the agent workflow GitHub
gitlab-pipeline adds agent:<role> and runs the agent pipeline GitLab
command marks the task, runs start_command with {number} {id} {ref} {role} {title} {url} {tracker} {harness} any tracker, when start_command is set
print marks the task and prints how to start it in a session the other trackers

Labels

Label Meaning
agent:<role> the task runs on that role; on GitHub adding it starts the agent
agent:team GitHub: one coordinator runs the roles of the Roles: line (GitLab: AI_FLOW_ROLES)
agent:split GitHub: Claude proposes a split in a comment (GitLab: SPLIT_ISSUE)
hold dispatch never starts this task
alignment-needed the merge request changes something other roles rely on
ai-review two reviews of the pull request, rules and spec

CI secrets and variables

Name Where Used by
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN GitHub secret, GitLab variable Claude Code jobs
OPENAI_API_KEY secret / variable Codex jobs
CODEX_MODEL GitHub variable Codex model (empty: Codex's default)
AGENT_PR_TOKEN GitHub secret Codex pull requests that start the CI
OPENCODE_MODEL, provider keys variable, secrets OpenCode jobs
AGENT_RUNNERS, AGENT_DEFAULT_RUNNER GitHub variables which tool runs which role
AGENT_AUTODISPATCH, AGENT_DISPATCH_TOKEN GitHub variable, secret dispatch at every merge
AGENT_DISPATCH_PER_ROLE, AGENT_DISPATCH_MAX GitHub variables its limits (1 and 3)
GITLAB_ACCESS_TOKEN GitLab variable splits; Codex and OpenCode merge requests

Where the tools find things

Claude Code Codex OpenCode
Project rules CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md AGENTS.md AGENTS.md
Roles .claude/agents/*.md .codex/agents/*.toml .opencode/agents/*.md
Skills .claude/skills/ .agents/skills/ .claude/skills/ or .agents/skills/
Forbidden commands .claude/settings.json .codex/rules/agent-team.rules permission in opencode.json and agents
Hooks .claude/settings.json → scripts/hooks/ .codex/hooks.json → scripts/hooks/ none
Settings .claude/settings.json .codex/config.toml opencode.json

Token costs

What every agent reads on every turn costs on every request: AGENTS.md (about 1,200 tokens after setup), CLAUDE.md, the descriptions of the agents and skills of the tool in use, and the tools of active MCP servers. Role prompts, specs and docs/agents/ cost only when an agent opens them. Files of other tools, trackers and workflows cost nothing unless an agent searches or opens them: the profile removes them anyway, so no agent stumbles on instructions for tools you do not have.

To keep costs down: one task per session, handoff notes instead of long sessions, MCP servers only on the agents that need them, and few skills per role.

This manual

The manual is written in Markdown, one file per chapter in docs/manual/. docs/manual.html is generated from those files and never edited by hand:

pip install markdown==3.11.2
python3 scripts/build_manual.py           # regenerate docs/manual.html
python3 scripts/build_manual.py --check   # fails if the HTML is not built from the current Markdown

The HTML records a hash of the Markdown it was built from; --check compares it with the files, and the repository's CI runs it on every pull request. To check before every commit: git config core.hooksPath .githooks.

Generated from the Markdown sources in docs/manual/.
